page_hint: Ch 2 §6, Architecture Consequence, prefill levers bullet
chapter: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: Changing format at the same byte width (BF16 in place of FP16) changes neither the bytes stored nor the H100 dense tensor-core peak: it trades mantissa bits (10 → 8) for exponent range
observed: The text says BF16 trades mantissa bits from 10 to 8 relative to FP16. BF16 has 7 explicit fraction bits (8 bits of significand precision including the implicit leading bit), while FP16 has 10 explicit fraction bits (11 bits of significand precision). The stated 10 → 8 is not the correct bit accounting.
evidence: IEEE 754 binary16: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 fraction bits. bfloat16: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 fraction bits. If counting significand precision including the implicit bit, the comparison is 11 → 8, not 10 → 8. The manuscript's own point — that BF16 and FP16 have the same byte width and the same H100 dense tensor-core peak — is correct, but the mantissa-bit parenthetical is numerically wrong.
root_cause: The parenthetical conflates explicit fraction bits with total significand precision and uses an incorrect BF16 fraction-bit count.
correction: Replace “trades mantissa bits (10 → 8) for exponent range” with an accurate statement, e.g. “trades fraction bits (10 → 7) for exponent range” or “trades significand precision (11 → 8 bits including the implicit leading bit) for exponent range.”
acceptance_test: Verify the revised sentence against IEEE 754 binary16 and bfloat16 definitions; the stated bit counts must match the standard and must not imply BF16 has 8 explicit fraction bits.

page_hint: Ch 2 §3, Prefill FLOPs bullet; Ch 2 §6, prefill levers bullet
chapter: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: a lower-precision path with a higher tensor-core peak (FP8/FP4)
observed: The canonical hardware is an H100. H100 tensor cores support FP8 but not FP4. Listing FP4 as a latency lever in the H100-based canonical discussion can mislead the reader into thinking FP4 is available on the stated hardware.
evidence: NVIDIA H100 supports FP8 tensor-core operation; FP4 tensor-core support is a later-generation (Blackwell-class) capability. The manuscript elsewhere correctly treats H100 FP8 as a higher-throughput path, but does not qualify FP4 as unavailable on H100.
root_cause: The lever list mixes a generic future precision option with the specific H100 canonical hardware without a hardware-support qualifier.
correction: Either remove FP4 from the H100-specific lever list or qualify it explicitly: “FP8 on H100; FP4 only on hardware generations that support it.” Apply the same qualification wherever FP4 is listed as a lever in the canonical H100 discussion.
acceptance_test: Search the chapter for “FP4” and confirm every occurrence is either removed from the H100-specific discussion or explicitly scoped to hardware that supports FP4.

chapter: Chapter 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference
quoted_clause: or fewer input tokens (retrieval quality, prefix reuse)
observed: Prefix reuse is listed as a way to reduce input tokens. Prefix caching/KV reuse does not reduce the number of input tokens in the request; it avoids recomputing K/V for a shared prefix. It can reduce effective prefill compute, but the prompt still contains those tokens and they may still be billed depending on provider policy.
evidence: The manuscript itself defines prefix caching in Ch 2 §1 as “reusing already-computed K/V for a shared prefix, to skip re-prefilling it,” not as reducing token count. The same chapter’s vocabulary table distinguishes prefix caching from token-count reduction.
root_cause: The sentence conflates reducing prefill work with reducing the number of input tokens.
correction: Rewrite to separate the levers: “fewer input tokens (retrieval quality, context compression) or less prefill work for the same tokens (prefix reuse).”
acceptance_test: Confirm the revised sentence no longer claims prefix reuse reduces input-token count, and that it is consistent with the Ch 2 vocabulary table’s definition of prefix caching.

page_hint: Ch 4 §6, Architecture Consequence, Economic feasibility bullet
chapter: Chapter 4 — The Anatomy of an AI Workload
quoted_clause: if the input token count could be reduced to 2 K (e.g. tighter retrieval/reranking to fewer chunks, context compression, or prefix caching), cost per request drops to ~$0.003
observed: Prefix caching is listed as a way to reduce the input token count. It does not reduce the number of input tokens; it reuses previously computed K/V for a shared prefix. It may reduce compute and, under some provider pricing schemes, reduce billed cost for cached tokens, but it is not a token-count reduction mechanism.
evidence: Ch 2 §1 defines prefix caching as reusing already-computed K/V for a shared prefix to skip re-prefilling it. Ch 4’s own cost calculation is based on input-token count times a per-million-token price; reducing recomputation is not the same as reducing the token count in the prompt.
root_cause: The economic example conflates prefill-compute reduction with input-token-count reduction.
correction: Remove prefix caching from the parenthetical list of token-count reducers, or rewrite the sentence to distinguish “fewer input tokens (retrieval/reranking, context compression)” from “lower effective prefill cost for the same tokens (prefix caching, if the provider prices cached tokens favorably).”
acceptance_test: Verify that the revised passage does not claim prefix caching reduces input-token count and that any cost claim for prefix caching is explicitly tied to provider pricing or compute savings rather than token-count reduction.

quoted_clause: The architecture is memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point ... the ~18.6× prefill oversubscription at the 40 rps peak (40 × 1.29 ≈ 51.6 PFLOP/s vs the ~2.77 PFLOP/s host capacity)
observed: The 18.6× figure is demand versus ONE 8×H100 host's sustained prefill capacity, not versus the deployed fleet. At 10 rps the same arithmetic gives 10 × 1.29 = 12.9 PFLOP/s, which is already 4.66× one host's 2.77 PFLOP/s. If the 10 rps design point uses H hosts, the 40 rps fleet oversubscription is 51.6/(H × 2.77), not 18.6× unless H = 1. The mini-case therefore mixes per-host capacity with fleet-level oversubscription and contradicts its own 'compute-sane at 10 rps' claim.
root_cause: Denominator/population conflation: per-host capacity versus deployed fleet capacity.
correction: State the number of hosts at the 10 rps design point. Compute required host-equivalents at 10 rps (4.7) and 40 rps (18.6), and report fleet oversubscription as 18.6/H. Alternatively, explicitly say '18.6 host-equivalents of prefill capacity' rather than '18.6× oversubscription'.
acceptance_test: Recompute the mini-case with an explicit H. Show that 10 rps demand is 12.9 PFLOP/s, 40 rps demand is 51.6 PFLOP/s, and the fleet oversubscription at peak is 51.6/(H × 2.77). The text must not call 18.6× a fleet oversubscription unless H = 1.

quoted_clause: the prefill pass for 9,200 input tokens costs ≈ 2 ×70e9 params × 9.2e3 tokens ≈ 1.29 PFLOP of linear (2PL) FLOPs (the quadratic attention term adds ≈ 0.2 PFLOP at 9.2K — ≈ 1.5 PFLOP full-square total ...), which against the ~1.08 s prefill budget implies a required rate of ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS
observed: The text computes 1.29 PFLOP for linear layers, then acknowledges ≈1.5 PFLOP full-square total including attention, but uses 1.29 PFLOP to derive 1.19 PFLOPS and later 51.6 PFLOP/s. The full-square prefill demand is 1.5/1.08 ≈ 1.39 PFLOPS, and 40 rps × 1.5 PFLOP ≈ 60 PFLOP/s. The table's 'Demand' column is therefore understated by about 17% if it is meant to represent the full prefill pass.
root_cause: Inconsistent scope: linear-only screening numbers are presented as full prefill demand.
correction: Either use 1.5 PFLOP, 1.39 PFLOPS, and 60 PFLOP/s throughout, or label every downstream number explicitly as 'linear-only screening' and keep the attention term separate. Table 6-1 should state which scope its Demand column uses.
acceptance_test: Recompute 1.5/1.08 and 40 × 1.5. The table and prose must agree on whether the quoted demand includes the quadratic attention term.
